subject: ela
cluster: Research to build and present knowledge
skillName: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts
intro: Each item gives you a full passage, then asks you to evaluate the evidence. For a stated analytical point, decide which quotation gives the strongest, most direct support, judge which explanation best shows how a quotation proves a claim, choose between two on-topic quotations, or spot a claim the passage never supports. Write the letter or sentence you choose, then briefly explain your reasoning.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

When the river flooded, the town of Cedar Hollow had only three days to act. The mayor went on the radio asking for help, but few people thought one announcement would matter. By dawn the next morning, though, the high school parking lot had filled with cars. Teenagers stacked sandbags in long lines that wound down to the water. Older residents who could not lift the bags brought coffee, blankets, and hot food, and they tracked which streets still needed crews. A retired engineer drew a map showing where the water would rise first, and dozens of strangers followed his plan without argument. By the time the river crested, the levee held, and no home on Maple Street was lost.

Claim: The passage shows that the people of Cedar Hollow succeeded because they worked together, not because of any single leader.

Which quotation is the STRONGEST evidence for this claim?
A) "The mayor went on the radio asking for help."
B) "Teenagers stacked sandbags in long lines, older residents tracked streets, and dozens of strangers followed his plan without argument."
C) "When the river flooded, the town of Cedar Hollow had only three days to act."
D) "A retired engineer drew a map showing where the water would rise first."
items.answer: B) "Teenagers stacked sandbags in long lines, older residents tracked streets, and dozens of strangers followed his plan without argument."

steps: The claim has two parts: the town succeeded by working TOGETHER, and not because of one leader. The strongest evidence must show many different people contributing.
Option B names several groups (teenagers, older residents, strangers) all acting at once, which directly proves a shared, group effort.
Option A points to one leader, the mayor, which works against the 'not one leader' part of the claim. Option D also centers one person, the engineer.
Option C only sets the scene of a flood and says nothing about teamwork.
B is the only quotation that shows the whole community combining its efforts, so it most directly supports both parts of the claim.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

Darnell had never spoken in front of the class without his notecards. For the science fair, his teacher told him the cards were not allowed. The night before, he practiced in front of the mirror until his words ran smooth, then practiced again for his little sister until she fell asleep. In the morning his hands shook, and twice he forgot a word and had to pause. But each time he paused, he took a breath, looked back at his poster, and found the next idea on his own. When he finished, he realized he had not glanced down once for a card that was not there. Walking back to his seat, he was already thinking about the history report due next week, the one he had been dreading.

Claim: Darnell grows more self-reliant over the course of the passage.

Which detail best supports this analysis?
A) "His teacher told him the cards were not allowed."
B) "In the morning his hands shook, and twice he forgot a word."
C) "Each time he paused, he took a breath, looked back at his poster, and found the next idea on his own."
D) "He was already thinking about the history report due next week."
items.answer: C) "Each time he paused, he took a breath, looked back at his poster, and found the next idea on his own."

steps: Self-reliant means handling things on his own. The best evidence shows Darnell recovering without his usual crutch, the notecards.
Option C shows him pausing and finding the next idea himself, which is exactly Darnell depending on his own skill instead of the cards.
Option A is the teacher setting a rule, not Darnell relying on himself. Option B shows him struggling but not yet overcoming it.
Option D shows him worried about a future report, which speaks to a new fear, not to growing self-reliance.
C directly demonstrates the trait the claim names, so it is the strongest support.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

For years, scientists believed octopuses acted purely on instinct. Newer studies tell a different story. In one experiment, an octopus learned to open a sealed jar to reach a crab inside, and after solving it once, it opened the next jar far faster. Other octopuses watched a trained octopus choose a red ball over a white one, then made the same choice themselves without any reward, suggesting they learned by observing. Researchers have even recorded octopuses carrying coconut-shell halves across the seafloor to assemble later as portable shelters, a kind of planning ahead. Each of these behaviors, scientists argue, points beyond fixed instinct toward flexible problem solving.

Claim: The passage supports the idea that octopuses can solve problems in flexible, intelligent ways rather than acting only on instinct.

Which quotation provides the STRONGEST evidence for this claim?
A) "For years, scientists believed octopuses acted purely on instinct."
B) "An octopus learned to open a sealed jar, and after solving it once, it opened the next jar far faster."
C) "Octopuses carrying coconut-shell halves across the seafloor."
D) "Other octopuses watched a trained octopus choose a red ball over a white one."
items.answer: B) "An octopus learned to open a sealed jar, and after solving it once, it opened the next jar far faster."

steps: The claim is about flexible, intelligent problem solving that goes beyond instinct. The strongest evidence shows an octopus learning and improving.
Option B shows the octopus solving a problem and then doing it faster the next time, which proves it learned, the clearest sign of flexible intelligence.
Option A states the old belief the passage argues against, so it supports the opposite of the claim.
Options C and D are on topic but incomplete on their own. C describes carrying shells without showing the planning, and D describes watching without showing the octopus then choosing successfully.
B most directly and completely demonstrates intelligent problem solving, so it is the strongest.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

The lighthouse had been dark for sixty years, but Nina's grandmother spoke of it as if it still turned. "On clear nights," she would say, "the beam swept the whole bay, and every captain knew he was not alone." Nina climbed the rusted stairs alone one evening, expecting nothing. At the top, the great lamp sat cold and cracked, wrapped in dust. Yet through the cracked glass she could see the lights of fishing boats far out on the water, small and steady. She thought of all the sailors her grandmother had described, and for a moment the dark lamp seemed less like a ruin and more like a promise that someone, somewhere, was still watching the water.

A student wants to support this claim: Nina comes to feel connected to people she has never met. They choose this quotation: "She thought of all the sailors her grandmother had described, and the dark lamp seemed less like a ruin and more like a promise that someone, somewhere, was still watching the water."

Which explanation BEST shows how the quotation supports the claim?
A) The quotation describes a lighthouse that has been dark for sixty years, which proves the building is very old.
B) The quotation retells the whole story of Nina climbing the stairs and looking out at the boats.
C) Nina's thoughts move from the strangers her grandmother described to a feeling that someone is still watching, showing she now feels linked to those distant sailors and watchers.
D) The quotation shows that Nina enjoys visiting old buildings and exploring on her own.
items.answer: C) Nina's thoughts move from the strangers her grandmother described to a feeling that someone is still watching, showing she now feels linked to those distant sailors and watchers.

steps: A good explanation connects the exact words of the quotation to the claim, which is about feeling connected to people she has never met.
Option C points to the specific shift in Nina's thoughts, from distant strangers to a sense of shared watching, which is precisely the connection the claim names.
Option A explains the building's age, not Nina's feelings, so it is off topic.
Option B just summarizes the events instead of showing how the words prove the claim.
Option D adds an outside guess about Nina liking old buildings, which the claim is not about.
C is the only explanation that links the quotation's wording to the feeling of connection, so it is best.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

Many people assume bats are blind, but the truth is more surprising. Most bats see about as well as humans do in dim light, and fruit bats see colors that help them find ripe food. What makes bats famous, though, is a second sense called echolocation. A hunting bat sends out high squeaks, far too high for people to hear, and listens for the echoes that bounce back from insects. From the time an echo takes to return, the bat can tell how far away a moth is, and from tiny changes in the echo it can even sense the moth's shape and movement. Using this, a single bat can catch hundreds of insects in one night, in total darkness, without ever bumping a branch.

Claim: Bats are blind and rely only on hearing.

Which part of the passage shows that this claim is NOT supported?
A) "A hunting bat sends out high squeaks and listens for the echoes that bounce back."
B) "Most bats see about as well as humans do in dim light, and fruit bats see colors."
C) "A single bat can catch hundreds of insects in one night, in total darkness."
D) "From the time an echo takes to return, the bat can tell how far away a moth is."
items.answer: B) "Most bats see about as well as humans do in dim light, and fruit bats see colors."

steps: The claim says bats are blind. To show it is unsupported, find the line proving bats can actually see.
Option B states that most bats see as well as humans in dim light and that fruit bats see colors, which directly contradicts the idea that bats are blind.
Options A and D describe echolocation, which is real but does not disprove the 'blind' part; they could even be misread as supporting 'rely only on hearing.'
Option C says bats hunt in darkness, which might seem to back the claim rather than refute it.
B is the only quotation that proves bats can see, so it shows the claim is not supported.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

Theo entered the chess tournament certain he would lose. His first opponent was last year's champion, a girl named Priya who never seemed to think before moving. Theo planned every move three turns ahead, scribbling notes between rounds, while Priya hummed and moved fast. He lost his first two games and wanted to quit. But after each loss he studied the board, asking Priya why she had made each choice, and she explained without bragging. In his fourth game, against a different player, Theo saw a trap forming the way Priya would have, and he avoided it. He did not win the tournament, but he left understanding the game in a way he never had before.

Claim: Theo values learning more than winning.

The passage contains two on-topic quotations. Which is the STRONGER evidence for the claim?
A) "His first opponent was last year's champion, a girl named Priya."
B) "After each loss he studied the board, asking Priya why she had made each choice."
C) "He did not win the tournament, but he left understanding the game in a way he never had before."
D) "He lost his first two games and wanted to quit."
items.answer: C) "He did not win the tournament, but he left understanding the game in a way he never had before."

steps: The claim is that Theo values learning over winning. Two quotations touch this: B and C. We must judge which is stronger.
Option C directly contrasts not winning with gaining understanding, and shows Theo treating the new understanding as the real reward, which proves he values learning above winning.
Option B shows Theo learning from his losses, which is good evidence, but it does not weigh learning against winning the way the claim does.
Option A only introduces an opponent, and Option D shows discouragement, neither of which supports valuing learning.
Because the claim is specifically about valuing learning MORE than winning, C, which sets the two side by side, is the stronger evidence.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

Cities around the world are planting trees to fight summer heat, and the results are measurable. On a hot day, pavement and rooftops can climb far hotter than the air, turning a neighborhood into what scientists call a heat island. Trees cool the air in two ways. Their leaves throw shade that keeps sidewalks and walls from soaking up the sun, and they release water vapor that lowers the temperature around them, much as sweat cools skin. In one study, streets lined with mature trees measured up to nine degrees cooler than nearby treeless streets at midday. Researchers add that the same trees trap dust, muffle traffic noise, and give birds a place to nest, but it is the cooling that has cities planting fastest.

Research question: How do trees lower the temperature in hot city neighborhoods?

Which quotation is the STRONGEST evidence answering this question?
A) "The same trees trap dust, muffle traffic noise, and give birds a place to nest."
B) "Their leaves throw shade and they release water vapor that lowers the temperature around them."
C) "Cities around the world are planting trees to fight summer heat."
D) "Pavement and rooftops can climb far hotter than the air, turning a neighborhood into a heat island."
items.answer: B) "Their leaves throw shade and they release water vapor that lowers the temperature around them."

steps: The research question asks HOW trees lower temperature. The strongest evidence names the actual cooling mechanisms.
Option B states both methods, shade and releasing water vapor, which directly answers how trees cool the air.
Option A lists other benefits like trapping dust and noise, which are true but do not answer the cooling question.
Option C explains why cities plant trees, not how trees cool. Option D describes the heat problem, not the trees' solution.
Only B explains the mechanism the question asks about, so it is the strongest evidence.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

The old clock shop smelled of oil and dust, and every wall ticked at once. Mr. Alvarez, the owner, was nearly ninety and moved slowly, but his hands never shook when he held a tiny gear. "A clock is patient," he told the boy who swept his floors. "It does the same small thing, over and over, and that is how it measures a life." The boy thought this was just an old man's saying until the morning Mr. Alvarez did not come in. The shop stayed dark for a week. When it opened again, a niece stood behind the counter, winding each clock by hand, one after another, the way he had. The ticking filled the room again, steady and unhurried, and the boy understood.

Claim: The passage suggests that careful, repeated effort can carry on even after a person is gone.

Which quotation BEST supports this theme?
A) "The old clock shop smelled of oil and dust, and every wall ticked at once."
B) "Mr. Alvarez, the owner, was nearly ninety and moved slowly."
C) "A niece stood behind the counter, winding each clock by hand, one after another, the way he had."
D) "The boy thought this was just an old man's saying."
items.answer: C) "A niece stood behind the counter, winding each clock by hand, one after another, the way he had."

steps: The theme is that careful, repeated effort continues even after a person is gone. The best evidence shows the work going on past Mr. Alvarez's absence.
Option C shows the niece carrying on his exact patient routine after he is gone, which captures both the repeated effort and its continuation.
Option A sets the scene, and Option B describes the owner's age, neither of which shows effort continuing.
Option D shows the boy doubting, the opposite of understanding the theme.
C ties the repeated winding to its survival after Mr. Alvarez, so it best supports the theme.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

Honey never spoils. Archaeologists have opened sealed jars in ancient tombs, thousands of years old, and found the honey inside still good to eat. Three things protect it. Honey holds very little water, and the bacteria that spoil most foods cannot grow without water. Bees also add an enzyme that produces a tiny amount of hydrogen peroxide, which kills germs. On top of that, honey is acidic, and few microbes survive in an acidic place. Stored in a sealed container away from moisture, honey can outlast nearly any other food in a kitchen. Open a jar to wet air, though, and it can absorb water over time and finally ferment.

Claim: Honey lasts a long time mainly because bees seal it inside thick wax.

Which statement correctly evaluates this claim?
A) The claim is supported, because the passage says bees add an enzyme to the honey.
B) The claim is supported, because the passage describes sealed jars in ancient tombs.
C) The claim is NOT supported, because the passage credits honey's low water, its peroxide, and its acidity, never wax sealing it.
D) The claim is NOT supported, because the passage says honey spoils quickly in any container.
items.answer: C) The claim is NOT supported, because the passage credits honey's low water, its peroxide, and its acidity, never wax sealing it.

steps: The claim says honey lasts mainly because bees seal it in thick wax. Check whether the passage gives that reason.
The passage names three causes: low water content, hydrogen peroxide from an enzyme, and acidity. It never says wax sealing preserves honey.
Option C correctly notes the real reasons and that wax sealing is absent, so the claim is unsupported.
Options A and B call the claim supported, but the enzyme and the ancient jars do not prove the wax explanation.
Option D misreads the passage, which says honey lasts a long time, not that it spoils quickly.
C is the accurate evaluation.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

The storm had knocked out the power, and the campers crowded close to the one lantern in the big tent. Outside, thunder rolled and the wind pressed the canvas walls inward. Ms. Okafor, the counselor, did not raise her voice or rush. She handed out the dry blankets, counted heads twice, and asked each camper to name one good thing about the day. A younger boy began to cry, and she sat beside him and told a quiet story until his breathing slowed. When a gust tore loose a corner of the tent, she calmly showed two older campers how to re-stake it while she held the flap. By the time the storm passed, no one had panicked, and several campers said later they had not even felt afraid.

Claim: Ms. Okafor keeps the campers calm through steady, deliberate action.

Which quotation provides the STRONGEST evidence?
A) "Outside, thunder rolled and the wind pressed the canvas walls inward."
B) "She handed out the dry blankets, counted heads twice, and asked each camper to name one good thing about the day."
C) "A younger boy began to cry."
D) "Several campers said later they had not even felt afraid."
items.answer: B) "She handed out the dry blankets, counted heads twice, and asked each camper to name one good thing about the day."

steps: The claim is that Ms. Okafor keeps campers calm through steady, deliberate ACTION. The best evidence shows her purposeful actions.
Option B lists a series of calm, organized things she does (blankets, counting, redirecting attention), which directly shows steady, deliberate action.
Option A describes the storm, not her actions. Option C shows a camper's fear, not her behavior.
Option D shows the RESULT (campers not afraid) but not the deliberate action that caused it, so it supports a different part of the idea.
Because the claim names her steady action, B is the strongest, most direct evidence.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

When a wildfire swept through the hills, most animals fled, but the woodpeckers stayed. Months later, scientists studying the burned forest noticed something strange. The blackened, standing trees were full of new life. Beetles laid eggs under the loosened bark, and the woodpeckers feasted on them, raising more chicks than in unburned years. Bluebirds and owls moved into the holes the woodpeckers left behind. Wildflower seeds that had waited years in the soil, needing the heat of fire to crack open, now sprouted in the sunlight that reached the cleared ground. Within three springs, the burned slope held more kinds of plants and birds than the green forest beside it. Fire, the researchers concluded, is not only an ending but also a beginning.

Claim: The passage shows that a fire can help a forest become richer with life, not only destroy it.

Which quotation gives the STRONGEST evidence for this claim?
A) "When a wildfire swept through the hills, most animals fled."
B) "Within three springs, the burned slope held more kinds of plants and birds than the green forest beside it."
C) "The blackened, standing trees were full of new life."
D) "Beetles laid eggs under the loosened bark."
items.answer: B) "Within three springs, the burned slope held more kinds of plants and birds than the green forest beside it."

steps: The claim is that fire can make a forest RICHER with life, not just destroy it. The strongest evidence directly compares the burned area's life to an unburned area.
Option B states the burned slope held more kinds of plants and birds than the green forest, which is the clearest proof that fire increased the variety of life.
Option C is on topic but vague, saying trees were 'full of new life' without comparison or measure.
Option D names one detail, beetles laying eggs, which is only one piece of the larger point.
Option A shows destruction and flight, supporting the opposite idea.
B is the most complete, measurable support, so it is strongest.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

Grandpa Lewis kept a garden no one asked him to keep. The vegetables he grew were more than his small house could ever eat, and every Friday he loaded the extra into a wagon and pulled it three blocks to the food pantry. He never mentioned it. When his knees grew too stiff for the walk, the neighbors expected the garden to die. Instead, on the first warm Saturday, two teenagers from down the street showed up with shovels, and Grandpa Lewis sat in a chair at the edge of the beds, pointing and teaching. By June the wagon rolled to the pantry again, pulled now by younger hands. Grandpa Lewis smiled but said only, "A garden is a thing you hand to somebody."

A student wants to support this claim: Grandpa Lewis gives quietly, without seeking credit. They choose this quotation: "Every Friday he loaded the extra into a wagon and pulled it three blocks to the food pantry. He never mentioned it."

Which explanation BEST shows how the quotation supports the claim?
A) The quotation shows that Grandpa Lewis grew too many vegetables for his small house to eat.
B) The quotation retells how the teenagers came with shovels and kept the garden alive.
C) The words "he never mentioned it" right after his weekly trips to the pantry show he gave food away regularly yet kept silent about it, which is giving without seeking credit.
D) The quotation proves that Grandpa Lewis was a hard worker who liked gardening.
items.answer: C) The words "he never mentioned it" right after his weekly trips to the pantry show he gave food away regularly yet kept silent about it, which is giving without seeking credit.

steps: A strong explanation links the exact words of the quotation to the claim, which is about giving quietly without seeking credit.
Option C points to the specific words 'he never mentioned it' paired with his regular giving, which is precisely quiet generosity with no credit sought.
Option A explains why he had extra vegetables, not how he gave quietly.
Option B summarizes a different part of the story, the teenagers, instead of explaining this quotation.
Option D adds an outside judgment that he liked gardening, which the claim is not about.
C is the only explanation that ties the quotation's wording to the claim, so it is best.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

For most of history, mapmakers drew the world from the ground, guessing at distant coastlines from sailors' reports. Errors crept in everywhere. A coast might be drawn twice as long as it really was, or an island placed hundreds of miles from its true spot. Everything changed when cameras rose into the sky, first on balloons, then on planes, and at last on satellites circling far above. From orbit, a single photograph could capture an entire continent at once, its rivers and mountains exactly where they sat. Computers stitched thousands of these images into maps so precise that a hiker today can find a single trail junction on a phone. The old guesswork gave way to a view no traveler on the ground could ever have had.

Research question: Why did maps become far more accurate in modern times?

Which quotation is the STRONGEST evidence answering this question?
A) "For most of history, mapmakers drew the world from the ground, guessing at distant coastlines."
B) "A coast might be drawn twice as long as it really was, or an island placed hundreds of miles from its true spot."
C) "From orbit, a single photograph could capture an entire continent at once, its rivers and mountains exactly where they sat."
D) "A hiker today can find a single trail junction on a phone."
items.answer: C) "From orbit, a single photograph could capture an entire continent at once, its rivers and mountains exactly where they sat."

steps: The question asks WHY maps became more accurate. The strongest evidence names the cause of the improvement.
Option C explains that views from orbit captured features exactly where they sat, which is the reason maps grew accurate.
Options A and B describe the OLD, inaccurate methods and their errors, the opposite of what made maps accurate.
Option D shows a RESULT of accurate maps (a hiker using a phone), not the cause.
Only C gives the reason for the improvement, so it best answers the research question.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

The new student, Priscilla, said almost nothing for the first month. At lunch she sat at the end of the table, drawing in a small notebook she snapped shut whenever anyone leaned over. The other kids decided she was stuck up. Then the art teacher pinned the class projects on the hallway wall, and a crowd gathered around one drawing of the school courtyard, every brick and leaf exact, the light so real it seemed to fall across the paper. It was signed P. Reyes. The next day at lunch, three students slid down the bench to ask Priscilla how she had done it, and for the first time she opened the notebook on her own and turned it toward them.

Claim: Priscilla was not unfriendly but simply shy and unsure of herself.

Which detail best supports this analysis, rather than the idea that she was "stuck up"?
A) "The other kids decided she was stuck up."
B) "She sat at the end of the table, drawing in a small notebook she snapped shut whenever anyone leaned over."
C) "A crowd gathered around one drawing of the school courtyard."
D) "It was signed P. Reyes."
items.answer: B) "She sat at the end of the table, drawing in a small notebook she snapped shut whenever anyone leaned over."

steps: The claim is that Priscilla was shy, not unfriendly. The best evidence shows protective, nervous behavior rather than rudeness.
Option B shows her guarding her notebook and snapping it shut when watched, which reads as shy and self-protective, fitting the claim.
Option A is the other kids' wrong judgment, the very idea the claim argues against.
Option C describes the crowd at her drawing, and Option D is just the signature, neither showing her shyness.
B captures the nervous, private behavior the claim explains, so it is the strongest support.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

Venus is often called Earth's twin because the two planets are nearly the same size and are next-door neighbors in space. Yet a visitor would find Venus a nightmare. Its thick atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide, which traps heat so well that the surface stays around nine hundred degrees, hot enough to melt lead, day and night. Clouds of sulfuric acid blanket the sky, and the air presses down with ninety times the weight of Earth's, crushing the few probes that have landed within hours. Even the spin is strange. A single day on Venus lasts longer than its year. Scientists study Venus not because we could live there, but because it shows how a planet much like ours can become utterly hostile.

Claim: Venus and Earth are alike in nearly every way.

Which statement correctly evaluates this claim using the passage?
A) The claim is supported, because the passage calls Venus 'Earth's twin.'
B) The claim is supported, because both planets are neighbors in space.
C) The claim is NOT supported, because the passage shows Venus differs sharply in heat, air pressure, clouds, and spin, alike only in size and location.
D) The claim is NOT supported, because the passage says Venus is smaller than Earth.
items.answer: C) The claim is NOT supported, because the passage shows Venus differs sharply in heat, air pressure, clouds, and spin, alike only in size and location.

steps: The claim says Venus and Earth are alike in nearly EVERY way. Check whether the passage backs that broad statement.
The passage lists only two similarities, size and being neighbors, then many sharp differences: scorching heat, crushing pressure, acid clouds, and a day longer than a year.
Option C correctly notes the few likenesses and the many differences, so the claim is unsupported.
Options A and B treat the 'twin' nickname and shared location as proof of being alike in nearly every way, but those are just the two exceptions, not the whole picture.
Option D misreads the passage, which says the planets are nearly the same size, not that Venus is smaller.
C is the accurate evaluation.
